title: Two-Mirror Angle Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you turn one mirror-angle dial and see how many images two mirrors make, and which angles give clean patterns.
pitch: The whole first screen is one dial and one ink colour: two hinged mirrors, a lopsided hand-drawn mark between them and the ring of its reflections. Drag the dial and watch the ring grow, snap shut at 60 or 45 degrees, and tear open at 70. You leave knowing why a kaleidoscope uses certain angles, why the textbook count of 360 over the angle minus one is only part of the story, and why an odd number of slices leaves a seam.
firstMinute: A page-sized picture already runs: the dial sweeps slowly from 90 to 45 degrees and the ring of reflections of a lopsided mark grows from 3 to 7 copies while a row of pips counts them. The visitor grabs the dial and drags it; at 60 degrees the ring closes with no gap and the dial clicks, which is the first success. No reading is needed, and the explanations sit below the picture.
conceptsToLearn: a mirror flips left and right
whyNow: Timeless; the constraint of one dial and a single ink colour is felt at once, and the page respects it for the whole lesson (extra controls live behind a More toggle).

purposeDetail.concept: Two plane mirrors hinged at angle theta make a ring of reflections. When 360 divided by theta is a whole number n, the n copies of the object (the original plus n minus 1 images) tile the circle exactly, every copy alternately flipped. That is the dihedral symmetry of order 2n that two mirrors at 180 over n generate. Other angles leave overlaps or gaps, and an odd n leaves a seam where two same-handed copies meet.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most coverage is a single exam formula (360 over theta minus 1) with the edge cases glossed over or stated inconsistently, so learners never see why the angle matters or what goes wrong when it does not divide 360.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious teenagers and adults, physics and geometry students, and makers who build kaleidoscopes.
prerequisites: knows what a mirror image is
can read an angle in degrees
misconceptions: Any mirror angle gives a pretty kaleidoscope pattern.
The formula 360 over theta minus 1 holds for every angle.
More mirrors always means more variety rather than a fixed set of tilings.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Turning the dial from 60 to 70 degrees: the ring that closed perfectly tears open, because the angle no longer divides the full turn; then at 120 degrees the ring closes but a seam appears that flips handedness, so the angle must divide a half turn for a seamless view.
demos: Hinge and glyph: drag the dial, see images appear and count them with pips
Snap angles: click through 90, 60, 45, 36, 30 and compare the count with 360 over theta minus 1
Off-divisor angles: set 70 or 100 degrees and see overlaps or a gap
Odd versus even slices: 120 and 72 degrees show the seam, 90 and 60 close; try a mirror-symmetric mark to heal the seam
More: move the object, then fold into the round tube view that makes the classic wedge pattern
checkQuestions: How many images do mirrors at 40 degrees make with the object centred?
Why does 100 degrees not give a clean ring?
Why does a mirror-symmetric mark hide the seam at 120 degrees?

research.summary: Two independent exam-prep pages state the image-count formula N = 360/theta - 1 with 60 degrees giving 5 and 45 degrees giving 7. University talk slides and a Rutgers article tie two hinged mirrors at pi/p to the dihedral group of order 2p. The edge cases (non-divisor angles, odd slice counts) are described inconsistently across sources, so the lesson derives them itself by exact unfolding geometry and tests the code against the verified values, labelling edge cases as the page's own derivation. The brief's constraint idea held up; the only thing I could not confirm is a strict even-only rule, which one patent contradicts (odd counts close if the mark is mirror-symmetric).

facts.claim: For two plane mirrors inclined at angle theta, textbooks and exam-prep pages give the number of images as 360/theta - 1 (as of 2026-10-14).
The same formula gives 5 images at 60 degrees and 7 at 45 degrees (as of 2026-10-14).
Two hinged mirrors at angle pi/p (180/p degrees) generate the dihedral group of order 2p (as of 2026-10-14).
Brewster Society analysis: for a general (non-divisor) angle the farthest images are ambiguous and depend on the exit mirror. Reported, not confirmed.
A patent says an odd segment count produces a clean ring only if the primary image is mirror-symmetric. Reported by one result, unconfirmed; the lesson derives this itself.
For angles that do not divide 360 some images overlap and the count is the integer part of 360/theta; sources are inconsistent on odd cases. Reported, unconfirmed.
Mirror-bounded triangles correspond to wallpaper groups p3m1, p4m, p6m (Dunham). Reported, unconfirmed; optional extension only.

design.coreLoop: Drag the dial, see the ring and the image count change at once, predict the next snap angle, then answer a check question and see the page confirm it with the picture; the surprise at off-divisor and odd angles keeps pulling the visitor back to test one more angle.
sophisticationHooks: Exact unfolding geometry (not just the formula) so non-divisor and odd cases are drawn truthfully
Handed mark that shows reflections as flipped copies in one ink colour using a hatched versus solid fill
Seam detector that highlights where two same-handed copies meet
Round tube view that turns the ring into the classic kaleidoscope wedge pattern behind More
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: SVG ring of reflections with one dial, snap points, image pips, odd/even seam demo, four check questions, intro and explainer text, pure tested geometry module. Cut: three-mirror wallpaper groups, sound, sharing.
risks: Edge-case rules (non-divisor counts, odd slice counts) are not consistently stated by sources; the page must present them as its own derivation, checked by node tests against the verified values 60 -> 5 and 45 -> 7, and show unverified claims as 'as of 2026-10-14, per <source>' or omit them.
The Brewster Society page could not be opened (host not found), so its claims stay unverified.
The single-colour constraint limits showing handedness; the hatched versus solid fill and a flip-marked glyph must be tested for legibility and contrast.
Search summaries blended results, so the independent-agreement marks rest on the separate result entries only.

title: Constraint Writing Studio
plainSentence: A writing workspace that lets you draw a writing rule, such as no letter E, then checks your text live and exports the finished piece.
pitch: Spin for a rule from the French workshop tradition of constrained writing (no chosen letter, letters with no tails, words that grow one letter at a time, one vowel only) or pick your own, then write. Every letter or word that breaks the rule lights up as you type, so the constraint is felt in the first ten seconds. Finish and export your piece as a plain text file or an image card stamped with its rule.
firstMinute: The page opens with a rule already drawn (no letter E) and a short sample line in the editor, with the one banned letter highlighted wherever it appears. The visitor deletes the highlighted word, types a replacement and watches the counter turn to 'rule kept', then presses Spin to try a different rule.
whyNow: Timeless creative workbench; also answers the brief's call for an experience where a ridiculous constraint governs the entire interaction.

purposeDetail.output: A short piece of text (poem, sentence or paragraph) that provably obeys one chosen writing rule, saved with the rule stamped on it.
exportFormats: PNG card with the text and its rule

research.summary: Constrained writing is a documented tradition: a French workshop of writers and mathematicians founded in 1960 (Queneau and Le Lionnais) catalogued rules such as the lipogram, and the English novel Gadsby (1939) and Perec's La Disparition (1969) both avoid the letter e. Definitions of snowball and the so-called prisoner's constraint vary between sources (snowball can grow by a letter per word or a word per line; the banned letter list for prisoner's differs, and the status of i is unclear), so the studio states its own exact version of each rule and lets the visitor flip the contested choices. All checking is simple string logic that can be tested in node.

facts.claim: The Oulipo workshop was founded on 24 November 1960 by Raymond Queneau and Francois Le Lionnais (as of 2026-10-14).
Gadsby, published in 1939 by Ernest Vincent Wright, is a novel of roughly 50,000 words that avoids the letter e (a few slips are reported) (as of 2026-10-14).
Perec's La Disparition (1969) is written without the vowel e. Reported on Wikipedia pages only, so shown as 'as of 2026-10-14, per Wikipedia'.
Definitions of the snowball form differ: one reading grows each word by one letter, another grows each line by one word (as of 2026-10-14).

The prisoner's constraint bans letters with ascenders or descenders; one source lists b d f g h j k l p q t y, others classify some letters differently, and the status of i is unstated. Unconfirmed; the studio states its own set.
Ten sonnets of 14 lines with interchangeable lines allow 10 to the power 14 poems (Queneau). Reported by one source, and the arithmetic (10 choices for each of 14 lines) checks out.

design.coreLoop: Spin or pick a rule, write, watch violations light up and fix them, reach 'rule kept', then export; Spin again gives a new rule so each session produces a different small piece.
sophisticationHooks: Pure rule functions (letter ban, tail-less letters, snowball growth, one vowel, same first letter) with edge cases for accents, hyphens and apostrophes shown in a rules panel
Starter examples written by the team and checked by the very same functions in node tests
A harder 'strict' toggle (for example ban a second letter) and a rule-stamped image card as the keepsake
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: five rules plus a spin, live highlighter and counter, text and image export, rules panel with plain definitions and a short history paragraph. Cut: dictionary-based rules (replace each noun with a later one in a dictionary), saved drafts across sessions, sharing.
risks: Studio might be read as a tool: the keepsake export, the spin and the playful voice must carry it.
Rule definitions differ across sources; the page must state its exact version of each and mark the contested letter choices.
Perec and exact slip counts for Gadsby are reported by few sources; omit them or date them 'per Wikipedia'.
Another scout proposed an anagram lesson (Sealing Secrets With Anagrams); this candidate avoids anagram rules to keep the subjects apart.
Mostly encyclopedia sources; the brief's Are.na and itch.io pointers could not be searched there.

title: Ramsey Party Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you colour the lines between six dots red or blue and discover why a one-colour triangle can never be avoided.
pitch: Six dots, fifteen lines, two colours: you try to colour every line so that no triangle is all one colour, first on five dots (it works) and then on six (it never does). A guided ladder turns your failed attempts into the proof, so the pigeonhole argument feels obvious rather than memorised, and a final rung shows how fast the same question becomes impossible to settle by hand.
firstMinute: The first frame shows five dots in a ring with a red pentagon and a blue star already drawn and the words 'no one-colour triangle here'. A button adds a sixth dot; its new lines appear grey, and as the visitor taps lines to colour them, a glowing triangle flashes the moment one colour closes a triangle. First success: the visitor makes a triangle appear on six dots within seconds and cannot make it go away.
conceptsToLearn: A line between two dots can be red (the two people know each other) or blue (they are strangers)
whyNow: Timeless: a short, complete proof with a surprising edge (five is not enough, six is), and nothing like it in the build history. It also gives the pool a combinatorics lesson that is not about primes or number systems.

purposeDetail.concept: Ramsey's party problem: in any group of six people, either three of them all know each other or three of them are all strangers. Colouring the 15 pairs of a complete graph on six dots with two colours always leaves a one-colour triangle (R(3,3) = 6), while five dots can be coloured with none (a red pentagon and a blue pentagram).
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations state the pigeonhole step in one sentence and move on, so learners accept the result without feeling why a fifth dot's colouring escapes but the sixth's cannot. Being allowed to try, fail and see exactly which line closes the trap is what the page adds.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious teenagers and adults with no maths beyond school; teachers looking for a ten-minute proof activity.
misconceptions: Checking a few colourings and finding a triangle each time counts as a proof (it does not; the page contrasts a few tries with the exhaustive argument)
Showing six is enough also shows five is not (the lower bound needs its own example: the pentagon and pentagram colouring)
Red and blue mean friends versus enemies (they only mean know each other versus do not)
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Pick one dot. It has five lines, and two colours cannot share five lines without one colour getting three. Look at the three dots at the far ends: any line among them in that colour makes a triangle with your dot, and if none is, they form a triangle in the other colour. Every escape route is closed.
demos: Rung 1: five dots with the pentagon and pentagram colouring already drawn; tap lines to try to break it and see that you cannot make a triangle without redrawing
Rung 2: add a sixth dot and try to colour its five new lines without making a triangle; a live hint highlights the line that always loses
Rung 3: pick any dot; its five lines fall into two colour bins and the bins visibly overflow at three (the pigeonhole step)
Rung 4: the three far-end dots light up and the visitor checks the three lines among them, ending in a red or a blue triangle in every case

Rung 5: a quilt view lays the 15 line colours out as a strip of 15 patches; a shuffle button tries thousands of random colourings and counts how many triangles each has, and the count never reaches zero
Rung 6: the same question with four-dot groups on 17 dots, shown as a pre-drawn colouring where no one-colour four-group exists, to feel why the next case is out of reach by hand
checkQuestions: Pick a dot on a seven-person party. How many lines leave it, and what is the least number that must share a colour?
On five people, colour the lines so that no one-colour triangle exists. Which two shapes do the colours draw?
Why does a single colouring of six dots that happens to contain a red triangle not prove the general statement?
If the lines among the three far-end dots are all blue, what triangle have you found?

research.summary: The statement, the pigeonhole proof and the pentagon-pentagram counterexample for five points appear in lecture notes, a maths-society blog and a problem-solving wiki, so the core is textbook-solid. The extension to four-person groups is also documented: a self-complementary colouring of 17 points with no one-colour four-group is the standard witness that 18 is needed. The whole claim for six dots is small enough (2 to the 15th = 32,768 colourings) that the page can ship a script-checked exhaustive count, so the lesson does not rest on search snippets alone. The idea of the minimum number of one-colour triangles in a six-dot colouring is attributed to Goodman in one search result only and is kept as optional.

facts.claim: Any red/blue colouring of the 15 lines between six dots contains a triangle of one colour (R(3,3)=6); the proof picks one dot, notes three of its five lines share a colour, and checks the lines among their far ends.
Five dots can be coloured with no one-colour triangle: sides of a pentagon in one colour and its diagonals (the pentagram) in the other, so six is the smallest number that forces a triangle.
R(4,4)=18: a two-colouring of 17 points exists (differences that are squares modulo 17 in one colour) with no one-colour group of four, and 18 points always force one.

Every red/blue colouring of the lines between six dots has at least two one-colour triangles (Goodman, case of six). Single search result; the page can instead show a count computed by the page's own exhaustive check.
Learners commonly check only the upper bound (six is enough) and skip the lower bound (five is not). Reported by a search summary of a college handout, not confirmed on the page.

inspirations: Ramsey's party problem as taught in discrete maths courses

design.coreLoop: Colour lines, watch the trap close, ask 'where is the escape', get the hint that names the dot with three same-coloured lines, then answer a check question. Each rung changes one thing (5 dots, 6 dots, the pigeonhole bins, the far-end triangle, a bulk shuffle), so the ladder keeps feeling like one idea getting clearer.
sophisticationHooks: A live pigeonhole view that groups the chosen dot's five lines into red and blue bins and flags the overfull bin
An exhaustive checker over all 32,768 colourings of six dots, run in a worker, which proves the claim in front of the visitor and lists the minimum number of triangles found
A quilt view that lays all 15 line colours out as a patch strip, so symmetry and the pentagon-pentagram pattern show as a repeat
A top rung that loads the 17-dot colouring and lets the visitor verify no one-colour four-group by a guided search
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: one SVG board with 5 to 6 dots, tap-to-colour lines, triangle highlighter, pigeonhole bins view, quilt strip, exhaustive checker, 6 guided rungs with 4 check questions, a short written explainer. Cut: seven or more dots beyond the single 17-dot display, user-entered graphs, accounts, sharing.
risks: The 'learners skip the lower bound' misconception comes from one search summary (verified:false); the page should phrase it as a general caution rather than a measured fact, or leave it out.
The minimum-two-triangles result is in one search result only (verified:false); the page should show the count computed in the browser, labelled as checked here.
The exact value of R(5,5) was not confirmed to a specific bound in the results seen (older bounds were quoted), so the page says only 'not known' with a dated source, or leaves it out.
Engineering: the 17-dot rung must be hand-checked by a script before shipping so the displayed colouring is truly free of one-colour four-groups.
Risk of looking like a puzzle game: keep the framing as a guided proof with questions, not a score.

title: Coastline Ruler Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you measure a coastline with shorter and shorter rulers, watch its length keep growing, then read off how wiggly it is.
pitch: You walk a ruler along a wiggly coast, shrink it, and see the length climb instead of settling, while a circle quietly settles to a fixed answer. A live chart of ruler size against measured length turns the climb into a straight line whose steepness is the coast's roughness (its fractal dimension), and you finish by ranking mystery coasts by eye and checking yourself.
firstMinute: The first frame shows a jagged coast with a ruler already walking along it in steps, a length readout, and a slider labelled 'ruler size'. Dragging the slider down makes the ruler re-walk the coast and the length number climb, with a second panel beside it where a smooth circle barely changes. First success: the visitor sees the same coast give 2,800 then 3,400 style jumps just by changing the ruler.
conceptsToLearn: Length can be estimated by counting how many equal ruler steps it takes to walk along a curve
whyNow: Timeless and very visual: it makes the coastline paradox a thing you do rather than a fact you read, and ends on a number (roughness) the visitor can measure themselves. It is a geometry lesson, not number theory, so it sits apart from the other maths candidates this round.

purposeDetail.concept: A wiggly curve such as a coastline has no single length: the measured length depends on the ruler. For a curve with fractal dimension D between 1 and 2, the measured length grows roughly like (ruler size) raised to the power (1 minus D) as the ruler shrinks, so a log-log plot of length against ruler size is close to a straight line with slope 1 minus D. A smooth curve has D = 1 and its length settles; the Koch curve has D = ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.26.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The coastline paradox is usually quoted as a fun fact and stops there. Few explanations let the learner do the measuring, see why the line on the log-log plot appears, and use its slope to get a number.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults and students aged about 14 and up, teachers, and anyone who has met 'fractals' as pretty pictures only.
misconceptions: A coastline has one true length that a good enough measurement would find
Smaller rulers just give a more accurate number of the same quantity, so the length must level off for every curve
Dimension has to be a whole number
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: On the log-log chart the points for the Koch coast fall on a straight line while the circle's line is flat, and the steepness of the coast's line is exactly the extra wiggliness the ruler keeps discovering.
demos: Rung 1: walk a ruler along a gentle curve and a circle; the length settles as the ruler shrinks
Rung 2: the same ruler on a jagged coast; the length keeps climbing and the visitor predicts the next value before it appears
Rung 3: build a Koch coast step by step and watch each stage multiply the length by four thirds while the ruler shrinks by a third
Rung 4: the live log-log chart appears and the visitor drags a fitted line through the points to read the slope
Rung 5: turn the slope into a dimension and compare the circle (1), the Koch coast (about 1.26), and a seeded random coast whose roughness the visitor guesses first
Rung 6: a 'zoom out, zoom in' toggle shows a real quoted example (Great Britain at two ruler sizes) with the figures labelled as quoted, not measured here
checkQuestions: If shrinking the ruler by half makes a coast's length grow by about 20 percent, is the coast smoother or rougher than the Koch coast?
Why does a circle's measured length stop changing while a jagged coast's does not?
Why is a log-log chart, not an ordinary chart, the right one here?
Can a curve have dimension 1.5? What would that say about it?

research.summary: The coastline paradox is documented in an encyclopedia article and several explainers: Great Britain measured with 100 km units is about 2,800 km and with 50 km units about 3,400 km. The ruler-length versus measured-length chart on log-log axes is described as a straight line whose slope gives the fractal dimension, which is between 1 and 2 for coastlines, and the Koch curve has dimension ln 4 / ln 3 (about 1.2619) with length growing by 4/3 at each stage. Richardson and Mandelbrot are the origin; one source quotes Mandelbrot's figure of about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain, which the page would only show as quoted. The model is exact for self-similar curves and only an approximation for real coasts, which the page must say.

sources.note: Not cross-checked against Richardson or Mandelbrot tables; these per-country figures are not used.

facts.claim: Measuring the coast of Great Britain with 100 km units gives about 2,800 km and with 50 km units about 3,400 km; the coastline has no well-defined length.
The Koch curve has dimension ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.2619, and its length grows by a factor of 4/3 at each stage so it is unbounded.
On log-log axes, measured length against ruler size lies near a straight line for a coastline, and the fractal dimension of a coast is between 1 and 2.

A coastline does not have a single well-defined length; the measured value depends on the ruler, and a smaller ruler gives a longer result (Richardson, then Mandelbrot's 1967 paper 'How long is the coast of Britain?').
Mandelbrot reported a dimension of about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain. Single result; show as 'as of 2026-10-14, per a spatial-analysis tutorial' or omit.

inspirations: Mandelbrot's 'How long is the coast of Britain?'

design.coreLoop: Shrink the ruler, predict the next length, see it, then watch a chart point appear. The next rung asks the visitor to fit the line and read the slope; a check question confirms the idea before the next curve.
sophisticationHooks: A correct divider walk (compass steps along the curve, each step a circle-curve intersection) so the ruler really walks the coast rather than being faked
Live log-log chart with a draggable fit line and a printed slope and dimension, rounded to the precision the data supports
Seeded random coasts with hidden roughness for a guess-the-dimension round with the answer revealed by measurement
An honesty panel: real coasts are only roughly self-similar over a limited range of ruler sizes, and the model is exact only for the built curves
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: Koch, circle and seeded midpoint-displacement coasts generated in the browser, divider-walk length function with unit tests, ruler slider, log-log chart with fit, 6 rungs, 4 check questions, explainer, and quoted Britain figures. Cut: real map data, country comparisons, user-drawn coasts (maybe a draw-your-own rung if time allows).
risks: Per-country dimensions (Australia, Norway, Portugal) came from one unreliable blog and are excluded; the Britain west-coast 1.25 figure is verified:false and must be shown as quoted or dropped.
Sketchplanations quoted about 3,500 km for the 50 km step against 3,400 km elsewhere, so the page says 'about' and cites the encyclopedia and one more source.
A course page gave the Koch dimension as 1.231; the formula ln4/ln3 = 1.2619 is used and the build should assert it in a test.
Looks like a fractal-pretty-picture page: the lesson must keep the chart and the slope reading central.
The coastline model is idealised; a real coast is not self-similar at every scale, and the page must say so.
The log-log straight-line claim rests on one search result (verified:false); the page demonstrates it with its own generated curves and labels the real-coast version as reported.
